The Blacktail butterflyfish Chaetodon austriacus is a conspicuous inhabitant of coral reef ecosystems across the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, where it maintains obligate associations with Acropora corals. Adults of this species attain a maximum recorded total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a modest body size relative to many congeners that reflects its specialized corallivorous feeding strategy. The total length at which individuals first achieve sexual maturity has been determined from field collections to be 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], indicating that puberty occurs at less than half the ultimate length. This relatively early onset of reproductive capacity is consistent with a life-history strategy favouring rapid generation turnover in an environment where coral availability, and consequently food supply, can fluctuate markedly. The corresponding wet weight at puberty was calculated from the length-weight relationship as 5 grams [Wwp = 5 grams], providing a useful metric for assessing condition and reproductive status in field surveys. These morphometric benchmarks are essential for constructing accurate demographic models and for evaluating the species vulnerability to habitat degradation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the embryonic development and hatching process of Chaetodon austriacus proceeds rapidly. The age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva through chorion rupture, was observed to be 7 days [ab = 7 days] at this same thermal regime at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of related species. This extremely small birth mass, characteristic of pelagic-spawning teleosts, underscores the substantial challenges faced during the early planktonic phase, including high predation risk and the need for rapid yolk absorption and commencement of exogenous feeding. The success of this early life stage is critical for population replenishment.

The maximum lifespan for Chaetodon austriacus has been documented at 9125 days [am = 9125 days] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], which corresponds to approximately 25 years. This extended longevity is notable among butterflyfishes and suggests a life-history strategy that balances a relatively slow pace of life with the ability to persist through periods of low coral cover. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This index, based on comparisons with the congener Chaetodon larvatus, provides a valuable baseline for assessing reproductive condition across seasons and in response to environmental stressors such as thermal anomalies.

The ultimate wet weight for adult Chaetodon austriacus is 50.3 grams [Wwi = 50.3 grams], a value derived from the species length-weight relationship and representing the maximum asymptotic body mass. In contrast to many reef fishes that exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, male and female blacktail butterflyfish converge on similar adult masses, likely reflecting the energetic demands of pair-bonded territorial defence. This adult mass of approximately 50 grams places the species within the typical size range for obligate corallivorous Chaetodontids, which generally exhibit modest body sizes optimized for manoeuvrability within complex coral matrices. The capacity to achieve such a mass depends critically upon the sustained availability of preferred Acropora polyps, and reductions in coral cover have been linked to declines in body condition and reproductive output. Seasonal shifts in prey quality may also influence growth trajectories.

The reproductive biology of Chaetodon austriacus is characterized by pair spawning within established territories, with gamete release coordinated around lunar cycles to optimize larval survival. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] and the maximum recorded longevity was 9125 days [am = 9125 days] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. Protecting the structural complexity of Acropora thickets is therefore essential for sustaining the long-term demographic stability of this iconic reef fish. Future work should examine how rising sea temperatures may influence these life-history parameters through changes in metabolic demand and food availability.
